text.p: Cambridge Shopping Centres Ltd on Monday launched a friendly C$375 million takeover offer for Markborough Properties Inc in a bid to increase sharply its ownership of malls across Canada.

The proposed merger gives Cambridge, which has interests in 45 Canadian shopping centers, holdings in 20 other malls. The deal is expected to increase its assets by more than 50 percent to about C$3.5 billion.
"It makes us a much larger, more dominant and more efficient organization in the industry," Cambridge Chief Executive Lorne Braithwaite told a news conference.

The Cambridge offer of C$375 million consists of about C$255 million in cash and C$120 million in convertible debentures of Cambridge. The offer works out to about C$0.46 per common share of Markborough.
Cambridge will also assume Markborough's debt, which is around C$1 billion.
Company officials said the merger was part of the growing consolidation of shopping center ownership across North America. The goal is to lower operating costs through greater economies of scale.
"This is no place for middleweights or lightweights and basically what we were was between a lightweight and a middleweight," Markborough Chief Executive Henry Ciocca told the news conference.

Markborough was financially hit by the recent recession and was selling non-core assets to pay down debt. The company therefore lacked the capital structure needed to pursue an aggressive growth strategy, Ciocca said.

"They (Markborough) were rapidly approaching the stage where they had to ask themselves, or the major shareholder had to ask himself, where was the growth potential for what remained of the company," said Harry Rannala, real estate analyst with Research Capital Corp.

Markborough was under pressure to realize value from majority shareholder Woodbridge Co, which owns 64 percent of Markborough's common shares. Woodbridge, which is controlled by Toronto's billionaire Thomson family, decided it did not want to infuse more capital into Markborough to pursue an acquisition strategy. The Thomsons are also the controlling shareholders of Thomson Corp.
Ciocca said Woodbridge had been a "long suffering and patient" investor and Markborough would not exist without the support of Woodbridge and the Thomson family.
Rannala, who maintained his buy rating on Cambridge, said the merger was positive for both companies, improving Cambridge's bottom line and reestablishing the company's growth momentum.
Cambridge shareholders appeared to approve the merger, with the company's shares closing up 0.80 to 10.50 on the Toronto Stock Exchange today on more than 200,000 shares.
Markborough fell 0.07 to 0.47, close to the price per share of the Cambridge offer.
